query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a dense, stable oxide coating (e.g., thin Al2O3 or Y2O3) to the as-cast HfNbTaTiZr surface will significantly reduce oxygen ingress and improve oxidation resistance at 1000 °C, thereby preserving the alloy’s 8–16% room-temperature ductility and 163–530 MPa yield strength at elevated temperature without sacrificing mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and 163–530 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C (strain rates 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1).
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin (1–5 µm) Al2O3 or Y2O3 layer by PVD, CVD, or a similar pack-cementation approach on HfNbTaTiZr surfaces to act as an oxygen diffusion barrier.
generation.conditions: Heat treatment at 1000 °C in air for at least 100 hours under strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
generation.structural_mediator: Dense ceramic coating that limits contact between the alloy substrate and oxygen at high temperature.
generation.mechanism: A stable oxide barrier restricts oxygen diffusion and thus lowers oxidative degradation of the refractory metal matrix, preserving strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, oxygen uptake is reduced by >80% at 1000 °C over 100 hours exposure, preserving the original 8–16% room-temperature ductility and an elevated-temperature yield strength of 163–530 MPa.
generation.baseline: Uncoated HfNbTaTiZr exhibits severe oxidation and loss of ductility at 1000 °C under similar exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: Coating efficacy may diminish above ~1200 °C due to potential spallation; protection over 300 hours or under thermal cycling conditions remains unverified.
generation.uncertainty: Little long-term data exist for coating stability or compatibility in thermally cycled or corrosive environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample groups of cast HfNbTaTiZr: one uncoated group and one group coated with Al2O3 or Y2O3 by PVD/CVD. Expose both groups to air at 1000 °C for 100 hours while periodically measuring weight changes and performing mechanical tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxide-coated group exhibits no significant reduction in oxygen uptake or does not maintain ductility and elevated-temperature yield strength better than the uncoated group, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. By combining refractory elements such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, Hf, …etc. in equi- or near equi-molar ratios, several RHEAs with promising mechanical properties have been reported [5] – [7] . However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties. decision.trend: Early work on cast Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti (2017) showed that refractory HEAs in this composition range can achieve moderate to high strength at elevated temperatures but offer limited oxidation/oxygen resistance. Later approaches for NbMoCrTiAl (2018) introduced in-situ ceramic phases to bolster high-temperature oxidation resistance while enhancing strength, though ductility was limited. More recently, Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi (2020) experiments explored interstitial modifications (adding O or N) for improved mechanical strength and damping, but oxygen-based modifications often reduced ductility and did not solve the oxidation challenge outright. None systematically applied a dedicated surface treatment solution for HfNbTaTiZr to counter oxygen ingress at 1000 °C without altering the bulk alloy composition.
decision.unsolved: A reliable high-temperature oxidation barrier for HfNbTaTiZr remains elusive. Previous studies either introduced interstitials (risking embrittlement), formed ceramic dispersions (changing bulk composition), or did not fully address long-term oxidation behavior at 1000 °C. A targeted surface-engineering approach for preventing oxygen uptake without sacrificing the intrinsic ductility and high-temperature strength has not been demonstrated.
decision.lever: Apply a dense, stable oxide coating (e.g., thin-film Al2O3 or Y2O3) via PVD, CVD, or pack-cementation on as-cast HfNbTaTiZr to create an oxygen diffusion barrier, then subject the coated alloy to 1000 °C exposure in air for >100 h at strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1
decision.why: Such a surface barrier directly tackles the oxygen-infiltration problem at high temperatures while preserving the alloy’s intrinsic mechanical properties. Prior work on refractory HEAs shows that interstitial control is key to avoiding embrittlement, and ceramic surface layers have successfully enhanced oxidation resistance in other high-temperature materials.
